results.abstract:
Sample return from the Moon’s South Pole-Aitken Basin (SPA) has been recognized as the highest priority lunar science mission for well over two decades, appearing as a recommended New Frontiers class mission in the two previous Planetary Science Decadal Survey documents (2003–2012 New Frontiers, 2013–2022 Visions & Voyages), and as a prioritized mission for the Lunar Discovery and Exploration Program (LDEP) in the 2023–2032 Origins, Worlds, and Life Decadal Survey (OWL). The South Pole-Aitken basin presents the ideal target destination to test nearly 60 years of lunar science hypotheses owing to a unique combination of its size, antiquity, and location on the lunar farside. Despite the recognized importance of SPA science, past sample return mission designs have been challenged by a combination of cost and technology.

This report defines science goals and objectives for a South Pole-Aitken Basin Sample Return and eXploration (SPARX) mission, the in situ and terrestrial laboratory measurements required for the completion of these objectives, and the lithologies, sample properties, and masses of samples that must be returned for the required measurements. This report also explores a range of potential mission implementation and programmatic architectures for achieving various levels of the SPARX science objectives, including a full range of mobility options, commercial capabilities, the role of astronauts, and the potential for multi-landing campaign-style science. From these investigations, the SPARX SDT has developed a baseline mission concept for a long- distance rover that would collect samples and conduct science at 21 locations across SPA before rendezvousing with Artemis astronauts for sample return. The proposed baseline mission includes a traverse design that can accomplish the SPARX science goals, optimizes the programmatic understanding of the implementation space, and fits within the cost guidance provided by NASA.

The return of samples from the Moon by the Apollo missions revolutionized not only our understanding of the Moon but also established the foundational lens through which we view the formation and evolution of the Solar System. And yet, as the field of planetary science has continued to evolve, with missions across the Solar System, comparative studies between planetary surfaces, and the re-examination of Apollo samples for a new generation, gaps in these initial models have begun to appear. The time is now, for a new generation of sample return, to address critical questions of Solar System and planetary formation, once again using the Moon as an archetype with scientific implications that will ripple across the rest of the Solar System.

results.title: Addressing Angular and Spectral Differences in Multispectral Sensor Intercalibration through a Spectral-Information–Driven Approach
results.abstract: This study introduces a novel methodology for inter-calibration between multispectral satellite sensors through the development of the Spectral Information-based Adjustment Matrix (SIAM) approach. SIAM simultaneously addresses discrepancies in sun-view geometry angles and spectral response functions (SRFs) between sensors by exploring spectral correlation relationships established across a wide range of viewing geometries and scene conditions. Such a scene dependent relationship can be adaptively and efficiently built by leveraging a high-fidelity hyperspectral dataset constructed for the Climate Absolute Radiance and Refractivity Observatory Pathfinder (CPF) mission. The approach is applied to ray-matched collocations of Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) and Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) inter-calibration samples. The results demonstrate that the SIAM approach can effectively characterize biases in MODIS–VIIRS inter-calibration caused by sun-view angle differences of only a few degrees, providing a novel solution to mitigate the angular matching challenge in multispectral sensor inter-calibration. The use of the SIAM algorithm to address SRF differences between sensors is compared with the well-established Spectral Band Adjustment Factor (SBAF) method. Excellent agreement in gain scaling factors derived from two independent approaches is confirmed. Linear regression analyses further verify SIAM’s capability to accurately estimate scene-dependent scaling relationships across key reflective solar bands under the assumption of negligible measurement offsets. SIAM provides a robust and efficient framework for operational inter-calibration of multispectral sensors.

results.title: Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances Site Assessment Progress Report (2026) South Repeater Building Solid Waste Management Unit 121 Kennedy Space Center, Florida
results.abstract:
This Per-and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances (PFAS) Site Assessment Progress Report (SAPR) presents the assessment activities performed at the John F. Kennedy Space Center (KSC), Florida, designated as Solid Waste Management Unit (SWMU) 121. The activities were completed at the South Repeater Building and surrounding area (Site) in February and April 2026. This PFAS SAPR was prepared by AECOM Technical Services, Inc. (AECOM) for the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) under Contract 80KSC019D0010, Task Order 80KSC021F0096.

The objectives of the additional PFAS assessment activities were to: (1) Continue to assess the extent of PFAS-impacted groundwater at the South Repeater Building area; and (2) Qualitatively and quantitatively characterize the potential migration of PFAS in environmental media (groundwater and surface water).  For the purposes of this report, groundwater results were compared to the November 2024 EPA National Primary Drinking Water Regulation Maximum Contaminant Levels (MCLs) for five PFAS compounds: PFOS, perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA), perfluorohexanesulfonic acid (PFHxS), perfluorononanoic acid, and hexafluoropropylene oxide dimer acid. For seven PFAS compounds without MCLs (perfluorobutanoic acid, perfluorobutanesulfonic acid, perfluorohexanoic acid, perfluorododecanoic acid, perfluorotetradecanoic acid, perfluoroundecanoic acid, and perfluorodecanoic acid), the November 2024 EPA Regional Screening Levels (RSLs) for tap water were used for comparison. Groundwater PFOS and PFOA results were also compared to the Florida Department of Environmental Protection (FDEP) provisional Groundwater Cleanup Target Levels (pGCTLs) released by FDEP in March 2022. Surface water results were compared to the FDEP provisional Surface Water Screening Levels (pSWSLs) also released by FDEP in March 2022. An additional 28 PFAS compounds without screening levels as of April 2026 were also analyzed for in groundwater and surface water.

In total, in February and April 2026, 112 groundwater samples and 9 surface water samples were collected to supplement the existing PFAS dataset. Sampling efforts are ongoing to further delineate PFAS impacts to the Site environmental media through DPT and monitoring well groundwater sampling and surface water sampling. Concentrations of PFOS, PFOA, and PFHxS in groundwater exceed the MCLs and/or RSLs. Concentrations of PFOS and PFOA are also greater than the pGCTLs in groundwater collected from the surficial aquifer system. The surficial aquifer system includes the shallow (6 to 17 feet bls), shallow intermediate (23 to 37 feet bls), deep intermediate (35 to 47 feet bls) and deep (55 to 59 feet bls) zones.  In surface water, concentrations of PFOS continue to exceed the Florida provisional surface water screening level. Surface water delineation efforts are ongoing for the drainage ditches to the west and south of the South Repeater Building. Historical comparisons of surface water and groundwater elevations from co-located staff gauge and monitoring wells indicate that the surface water ditches are losing streams where surface water seeps to groundwater. However, the borrow ponds data indicated that groundwater is typically higher in elevation than surface water, indicating groundwater upwells into the ponds.

The highest concentrations of PFAS in groundwater continue to be in the vicinity of the source area at 2 to 12 feet bls, as well as the area surrounding the borrow ponds approximately 730 feet northwest of the source area; the affected interval is approximately 6 to 27 feet bls. PFOS, PFOA, and PFHxS are the most prevalent PFAS compounds found in groundwater and surface water. Concentrations greater than 10 times the MCL are found within 800 feet west of Tel-4 Road. Data gaps appear to be vertical delineation west of the South Repeater Building in the former citrus grove area, with low-level concentrations (4.5- 20 ng/L) and within the vicinity of the South Repeater Building. The southern extent, along Tel-4 Road, of PFAS-impacted groundwater has been laterally delineated. Lateral delineation of groundwater was completed for the northern end of North Courtenay Parkway and on the north side of Tel-4 Road. Lateral delineation at the western boundary has been delineated within KSC boundaries. Vertical delineation has been completed to the confining unit in the northeast portion of the site.

results.title: 3D Body Scanning for Space Anthropometry: Technology Exploration and Development
results.abstract:
Exposure to different gravity environments induces physiological and biomechanical changes in the human body. Past space flight reported various observations, including spinal elongation, fluid shifts, muscle volume loss, and altered neutral body posture (NBP). Accurately capturing these changes is critical for human-system integration, space habitat design, and optimizing spacesuit fit. 

Historically, in-flight anthropometry during Space Shuttle and International Space Station (ISS) missions relied on manual measurements (e.g., caliper or tape measure based) or multi-view stereo photogrammetry. Although these multi-camera setups successfully estimated linear body dimensions (e.g., stature, shoulder height, torso length) and even NBP, they fell short of providing high-resolution 3D volumetric data directly comparable to ground laboratory reference body scans.

Deploying commercial off-the-shelf 3D body scanners in spaceflight or reduced-gravity training analogues presents significant technical challenges. Structure-from-Motion (SfM) scanners, such as handheld or turntable types, often require several minutes of scan time, which may be incompatible with a body floating in microgravity or transient gravitational cycles (20-30 seconds each) in reduced gravity simulation aircraft. Furthermore, space habitats or vehicles like Orion often do not have sufficient interior volume to set up a dedicated scan booth. Multi-sensor extrinsic calibration is extremely difficult to achieve and maintain due to misalignment from structural vibrations or physical contact from floating crewmembers. Lastly, the flight-ready certification process is a substantial huddle, regardless of the underlying scanner architecture.

While NASA has been continuously seeking commercial solutions, a recent in-house development effort has also demonstrated novel hardware and algorithm configurations tailored for 0-g and 1/6-g environments. The new prototype relied on a low-cost depth sensor paired with an RGB camera. An ArUco marker-based visual recognition method effectively eliminated the burden of extrinsic calibration and reliance on controlled manual sensor maneuvering operation as with the common handheld scanner. This architecture substantially reduces crew setup overhead and operational constraints. Although technical challenges still remain, proof-of-concept testing successfully verified that the prototype produces surface models comparable in quality to ground-based reference scans. 

Overcoming these operational hurdles enables rapid, reliable whole-body surface scanning in space flights and habitats. Beyond supporting traditional data needs for suit sizing and hardware design, 3D body scan can provide key medical monitoring biomarkers, such as non-invasive insights into fluid shift, muscle atrophy, and underlying musculoskeletal composition changes over long-duration missions. Furthermore, these scanning technologies have a significant potential for broader exploration needs, such as real-time interior occupancy analysis and Extravehicular Activity (EVA) operation planning.

results.title: In Flight Anthropometry and Health Surveillance for Future Exploration Missions
results.abstract:
As astronauts are exposed to microgravity the body shape and size change which can affect suit fit, health surveillance, and hardware configurations. Previous studies on the International Space Station (ISS) and Space Shuttle have shown up to 3% stature and 6% sitting height change can occur due to microgravity exposure (Young et al., 2020, 2021). While these studies provided critical data previously unavailable for space exploration, several limitations were also noted for Lunar and Mars Missions. Given the need for high-temporal resolution and future mission relevant anthropometry data which was not fully available in the past in-flight crew anthropometry studies, a new measurement initiative was recently kicked off with NASA. One of the key expansions for the new data collection is incorporating crew medical monitoring components in addition to the traditional focus for suit and hardware fit. This data will be used in conjunction with body mass to determine if there is any correlation between the two sets of data to assist in detecting health and body changes that may occur during future exploration missions where body mass hardware is not available. The timepoints were also adjusted to capture how quickly the changes might occur, changes prior to return to earth, and how quickly crewmembers’ recovery, with an aim to capture both the transient phase and steady-state phases of crew anthropometric changes. This is particularly important as the Lunar Missions involve more frequent gravity changes, such as 1-g to 0-g, then 0-g to 1/6-g.  

Ideally, this data would be captured using 3d scan technology as in the ground laboratory. However, due to constraints, manual measurements are currently being collected while scan technology is developed. As technology improves and potential hardware is developed that might work on ISS or lunar surface, ground-based efforts continue to collect scan data preflight and postflight. Continued effort has been in progress to identify the optimal technology for in-flight body scanning, which can substantially improve the data resolution matching the ground reference measurements.

results.title: Characteristics of Magnetic Sources During Solar Minima
results.abstract: A census of magnetograms acquired by the space-based Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager (HMI) during solar activity minimum between 2019 January 1 and 2020 February 29 reveals a population of small, typically ∼1 Mm across, predominantly unipolar magnetic sources, embedded in extensive same-polarity halos. The sources carry ∼10<sup>18</sup> Mx fluxes and have median lifetimes of 400–670 s. Some vary on ∼1 minute timescales, rapidly doubling their magnetic flux densities (MFDs), then returning to the preoutburst level. Emission from a slowly changing mix of network and small-scale sources modulates the total solar irradiance (TSI) at 0.005%–0.01% levels on rotational timescales. We find evidence of a nonlinear TSI–magnetic field relationship at very low activity levels. During the 2019 cycle minimum, as in the prior activity minimum in 2009, the total MFD in ground-based magnetograms measured by the Global Oscillation Network Group (GONG) persistently remained in excess of ∼1.5 G above that of the total flux in the Gaussian core. Using Wilcox Solar Observatory (WSO) synoptic photospheric magnetic field maps, we identify an overall decline of ∼2 G in total MFD from solar minimum in 1976 to the 2009 and 2019 minima, which we attribute to the decline of the Centennial Gleissberg Cycle of 1910 to 2009. We speculate that the MFD during the upcoming solar activity minimum in 2029 may be higher than in 2019 as the next Gleissberg cycle manifests.

results.title: Electron-Mediated Transport in Space, Astrophysical, and Laboratory Plasmas

organization.name: Dutch Institute for Fundamental Energy Research
Centro de Ciencias Ambientales EULA-Chile de la Universidad de Concepción

results.abstract:
Electron-mediated transport is fundamental to the thermal and dynamical evolution of plas
mas across a vast range of physical environments, from the solar wind and solar atmosphere
to astrophysical systems such as galaxy clusters and accretion flows, to laboratory and fusion
plasmas. This article reviews the current state of understanding of electron transport, draw
ing together observations, simulations, and theory to contextualise key challenges and open
questions. We characterise plasma environments using the Knudsen number and electron
beta, and highlight that some systems fall in an intermediate regime between the collisional
and collisionless limits. In the collisional limit, transport is well described by the Chapman
Enskog–Braginskii framework, yielding anisotropic heat fluxes and momentum transfer
rates governed by the ratio of the electron mean free path to the electron gyroradius. In
the collisionless limit, Landau-fluid closures and quasilinear wave–particle interaction the
ory describe heat flux regulation through resonant instabilities, particularly whistler-mode
waves, which suppress parallel electron heat flux below Spitzer–Härm predictions in high
beta plasmas. We review approaches to bridging collisional and collisionless regimes, in
cluding velocity-space-dependent collision operators, moment-based interpolating closures,
and data-driven methods trained on fully kinetic simulations. Comparison with solar wind
observations from the Parker Solar Probe and Wind missions reveals that the current at
tempts at bridging collisional and collisionless closures account for only limited regions of
parameter space, underscoring the need for improved models. Four central challenges are
identified for future transport theory: capturing the velocity-space dependence of collisional
and collisionless scattering, describing spatial transitions between transport regimes, incor
porating turbulence, and developing computationally tractable effective collision operators
for large-scale simulations.

results.title: MissionDPT: Simulation and Forecasting of Radiation Doses and Health Risks for Space Exploration Missions
results.abstract: Radiation exposure in space presents significant challenges to crew health and performance. To mitigate its impacts, research in space radiation environment, mass shielding geometry, nuclear interactions, transport codes and biological responses has been conducted for decades, offering many established models and codes. In this work, a web tool MissionDPT (Mission Dose Projection Tool) is reported which incorporates the most up-to-date version of these codes with simple input and output interface, enables interested users to calculate dose quantities and estimate acute risks for any low Earth orbits (LEO) and beyond LEO missions. Simulation results for dosimeters flown during the Artemis I and International Space Station (ISS) missions with known shielding files and trajectories are reasonably close to their measurements. A set of solar energetic particle forecasting models, University of Malaga Solar particle Event Predictor (UMASEP), are also integrated to provide dose information before or near the onset of solar particle events (SPEs). With archived Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellite (GOES) solar proton data from 1986 to present (real time data updated every 5 minutes), MissionDPT can be used either to analyze the radiation exposure and acute health risks for historical severe SPEs, or to serve as a console tool for flight operational team in contingent scenarios for the upcoming lunar and Mars missions.

results.title: A Review of Superconducting Electric Machines with On-Board Cryocoolers

organization.name: Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology

results.abstract: This paper reviews the evolution and emerging direction of superconducting electric machines that employ onboard cryocoolers integrated directly into the rotor, eliminating the need for cryogenic fluid coupling and, in some cases, rotary seals. Traditional low-temperature superconducting (LTS) machines relied on external cryogenic systems and liquid helium transfer couplers, which introduced excessive complexity, poor reliability, and significant parasitic energy losses. The advent of high-temperature superconductors (HTS) has enabled compact, closed-cycle cryocoolers that support self-contained, fluid-free refrigeration architectures suitable for rotating applications. This paper examines the key technological challenges associated with on-board cryocooler integration and reviews three representative efforts by KAIST, NASA, and Hinetics, each illustrating distinct strategies and milestones toward practical implementation. KAIST demonstrated early proof-of-concept for rotating machines with on-board cryocoolers, NASA developed a shaft-integrated Stirling-type pulse tube cryocooler for a 1.4 MW hybrid-electric motor, and Hinetics achieved full-scale validation of a self-contained HTS rotor incorporating a commercial Stirling cryocooler and spoke-suspension torque tube. Collectively, these achievements confirm the technical feasibility of on-board cryogenic refrigeration and highlight steady progress toward compact and efficient superconducting rotating systems across various applications. Embedding cryocoolers directly within the rotor enables practical, efficient, and commercially viable superconducting propulsion technologies.

results.abstract:
This paper focuses on comparing the computations performed by numerous international organizations to experimental data for the empty Virginia Tech Stability Wind Tunnel (VT SWT). The Virginia Tech team has conducted extensive experimental measurements of the VT SWT at Reynolds numbers of 1.7, 2.8, and 3.9 million per meter. Experimental data for predicted quantities such as wall pressure coefficient, wall boundary layers, and corner flow velocity magnitude have been released for the as-designed geometry (i.e., averaged over all 4 walls or all 4 corners). Experimental data for as-built geometry focusing on separate walls/corners has also been released. Also available are detailed inflow boundary conditions as well as geometry scans of the contraction, high-speed leg (i.e., the test section), and the diffuser. A systematically-refined family of 8 structured grids has been created for both the as-designed and as-built geometries. These grids do not include the diffuser and simply extend the test section downstream to provide an appropriate location for the outflow boundary condition. These grids range in size from ∼1.24 million cells on the coarsest grid to
∼638 million cells on the finest grid. Best practices for modeling subsonic wind tunnel facilities are presented.

results.title: Coordinated Analyses of an Agglutinate in a Mature Lunar Soil
results.abstract: Space weathering processes on the Moon such as solar wind irradiation and micrometeoroid bombardment result in the modified optical properties and chemistries of lunar soils. The spectral properties of space weathered lunar soils are largely determined by the formation of nanophase iron metal (npFe), which results in reduced reflectance, spectral slope reddening, and the attenuation of diagnostic absorption bands. NpFe occurs in rims on individual lunar soil grains and in impact-derived melt in agglutinates. Whereas individual lunar soil grains have been well-characterized to date, detailed characterization of agglutinates down to the nm-scale are currently lacking. Here we report early results on the coordinated analyses of an agglutinate in the mature Apollo 17 lunar soil 72501 using several electron beam techniques.

results.title: Introduction to the Special Issue on Advanced Air Mobility Noise: Predictions, Measurements and Perception
results.abstract: This Special Issue focuses on noise associated with Advanced Air Mobility (AAM), an emerging class of predominantly electric distributed-propulsion aircraft designed for urban and regional transportation. As these vehicles move toward certification and deployment, noise has become a central challenge for regulatory approval and public acceptance, particularly due to operations in densely populated areas and at low altitudes. The 24 contributions in this issue address three key aspects of AAM noise: prediction, measurement, and human perception. Prediction studies span a wide range of modeling fidelities, from high-resolution simulations to improved semi-analytical approaches, and examine complex aeroacoustic mechanisms including rotor interactions, turbulence ingestion, and broadband noise generation. Measurement studies, largely at model scale, provide new insights into tonal and broadband noise characteristics across configurations and operating conditions, while supporting model validation. Perception-focused contributions investigate annoyance, sound quality metrics, and auralization, emphasizing the role of context and operational factors in shaping human response.  Together, these works highlight the interdisciplinary nature of AAM noise research and the need for integrated approaches to enable quieter vehicle design.

Broadband Surface Albedo for Snow Derived From Satellite Observations
results.abstract: Spectral surface albedo depends on the surface type. Broadband surface albedo is calculated as the integral of the spectral albedo weighted by the surface downward irradiance spectrum. Consequently, unlike spectral albedo, broadband albedo depends not only on surface properties but also on atmospheric conditions, such as whether the sky is clear or cloudy. The difference between clear- and cloudy-sky broadband albedos is particularly significant for snow-covered surfaces for two main reasons. First, snow exhibits a strong contrast in spectral albedo between the visible and near-infrared (NIR) regions. Second, cloud absorption is stronger in the NIR, which reduces the surface downward irradiance relative to the visible region. When clouds are present, broadband snow albedo increases nearly 0.1 above clear-sky albedo. In the Clouds and the Earth’s Radiant Energy System (CERES) radiative transfer model, satellite-observed broadband surface albedos are used to constrain assumptions about surface spectral albedo. However, such satellite observations are available only under clear-sky conditions. The current algorithm, that derives the initial spectral albedo for the radiative transfer model, normalizes a cloudy sky spectral albedo to a clear sky broadband albedo derived directly from CERES observations. We find this normalization underestimates surface broadband albedo over snow and ice in cloudy sky conditions. We demonstrate that, even in the presence of clouds, because the numerator in the normalization is based on a clear sky observation, assuming an initial clear sky spectral albedo improves the representation of surface albedo for snow and ice under clouds.

Towards a Hazard Assessment Workflow for Assurance of Increasingly Autonomous Systems
results.abstract: The advent of increasingly autonomous systems poses a significant challenge for design assurance. As human operators are increasingly replaced by automated decision-making, the operational environment must be taken into account at design time. As a result, there is an increasingly large and complex input space to consider during design, and assurance approaches must be adapted to accommodate this paradigm shift. Existing safety assessment methodologies were typically developed for systems under continuous human supervision, and new approaches are needed to assure autonomous systems. In this article, we propose a hazard assessment methodology for the safety assurance of increasingly autonomous systems.  The workflow combines Natural Language Processing (NLP)-enabled elicitation of hazards from historical incident data, functional modeling, and scenario-based resilience simulation to augment traditional expert-driven hazard analysis and improve coverage of the hazard space. Requirements derived from this analysis are subsequently formalized in a structured natural language, enabling automatic generation of logical formulae, which can be analyzed for correctness. The framework is realized through two NASA-developed toolsets: the Hazard Analysis DESigner (HADES) and the Formal Requirements Elicitation Tool (FRET). The methodology is demonstrated on TROUPE, a NASA experimental rover swarm designed to autonomously and cooperatively map unknown terrain.

results.title: Polymer Composite Material Testing for a Cryotank Application
results.abstract:
Composite cryotanks will play a key role in enabling the next generation of efficient aircraft. Carbon fiber reinforced polymer (CFRP) composites have the benefits of reduced weight and potentially higher structural strength compared to traditional metallic fuel tanks. A material screening study was conducted to inform material selection for liquid hydrogen (LH2) fuel storage. Three composite materials were considered because of their aerospace grade toughness, strength, and existing data to compare against. These materials were a thermoplastic low-melt polyaryletherketone (LM-PAEK)/carbon fiber (CF), thermoset/CF, and hybrid thermoset/thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU) veil/CF composite. Mechanical screening tests included tension, compression, in-plane shear (IPS), and tensile-tensile fatigue (TTF). Each material was tested at both a baseline (no liquid nitrogen/LN2 cycling) and 100 LN2-cycled conditions to determine the knockdown factor, if any, of each material when exposed to environmental loading effects in a cryotank. Results show minimal effects of the LN2-cycling compared against baseline values. The three materials behaved similarly in tension; however, the thermoplastic/CF had the highest IPS toughness. The hybrid thermoset/TPU/CF composite had the lowest IPS strength, compressive strength, and toughness. LN2-cycling had minimal effects on tensile-tensile fatigue performance of the thermoplastic/CF material. Mechanical data was captured to guide material down selection for future commercially viable hydrogen aircraft design.

In its current state, there does not exist a consolidated, publicly available database for CFRP composite material performance data at cryogenic temperatures. The next step in this work is to test the thermoplastic and thermoset CFRP composites, as well as the neat resins, at LH2 relevant temperature (20 K) to capture this crucial material property data. These results are essential to inform cryotank design and modeling efforts. The process to start this next round of testing has begun. Planned mechanical tests include toughness (single-edge notched beam), tension (unidirectional and quasi-isotropic), thermal expansion, and thermal conductivity. Some tests will also be conducted at an intermediate temperature of 111 K relevant to liquid natural gas (LNG), another attractive fuel choice. The ultimate goal is to manufacture a sub-scale cryotank part that can pass relevant burst, fatigue, permeation, and thermal cycling tests. This work is a part of NASA’s Commercially viable Hydrogen Aircraft for Robust Growth in Efficiency (CHARGE) Project under the larger NASA Subsonic Vehicle Technologies and Tools (SVTT) Project.

results.title: The Contaminant Footprint of Landed Spacecraft: Toward an Inventory and Modelling Framework
results.abstract:
All spacecraft generate and carry contaminants, i.e., unwanted and potentially harmful material. When a spacecraft lands and operates in near-vacuum, as onto Earth’s Moon, it introduces contaminants into its environment that may compromise mission science objectives and engineering performance. Contamination of solar system bodies may irrevocably degrade targets of unique value to planetary scientists, for instance, as lunar landed spacecraft introduce propellant effluents into the otherwise pristine ice of the Moon’s permanently shadowed regions.

NASA’s planetary protection discipline seeks to ensure that solar system bodies are not contaminated, for scientific purposes, by terrestrial material (i.e., forward contamination). This interest aligns with planetary science interest in mitigating the transport of terrestrial contaminants onto solar system bodies and in controlling types of contamination that could compromise the scientific value of samples or measurements. NASA, and other entities that practice planetary science, have compelling and multidisciplinary interests in the preservation of special regions and sampling sites of high scientific value – including lunar permanently shadowed regions (PSRs) – from inadvertent contamination by any spacecraft, and in understanding the contamination of such regions by all spacecraft.

Organic molecular contamination here represents a primary threat. Organic molecules will be introduced to solar system bodies by nominal landed spacecraft and crew processes – including by the action of descent and ascent engines; natural materials outgassing; and crew environmental and life support system sources. Molecular contaminants can also travel in the free-molecular sense at global scale across near-vacuum bodies, including into regions where they may be permanently trapped.

This presentation will address a high-level study to identify sources of contaminants – in particular, organic material – generated by landed spacecraft along with the transport vectors by which these contaminants can reach sites of scientific interest on bodies like the Moon. A vision for an integrated modeling framework for the organic contamination footprint of spacecraft missions, individually and collectively, will also be described and presented along with initial conclusions related to organic molecular transport.

results.title: The Topology and Stability of Drops at Open Tube Ends
results.abstract: We numerically compute the configurations and stability of liquid drops at the ends of open right circular cylindrical tubes as a function of fluid properties, initial conditions, wetting and non-wetting contact angle, liquid volume, tube radius, and gravity vector. The results are presented as maps of drop topologies versus Bond number for liquid volumes either internal or external to the tube. We identify stable topologies that are highly exaggerated in low-gravity environments. Though observable in terrestrial experiments, such configurations and stability limits are uniquely insightful for the design and analysis of manual and automated wet lab unit operations such as pipetting aboard spacecraft.

results.title: Development of a Digital Twin for Electrified Aircraft Powertrain Health Management
results.abstract: The augmentation of aircraft powertrains with electrical power systems is a promising path to reducing aircraft fuel consumption, emissions, and noise. Like conventional propulsion systems, electrified aircraft propulsion (EAP) systems will be subject to wear and tear throughout their lifecycles. System health management for EAP will enable efficient flight and maintenance scheduling, realizing economic, safety, and reliability benefits. A digital twin is, broadly, a dynamically updated virtual representation of an individual physical asset. This paper presents a Kalman filter-based approach for the development of a digital twin for an electrified powertrain and applies the approach to an EAP controls testbed. Measurements from nominal testbed operations are used to update a nonlinear model of the testbed. A Kalman filter is then created and used to identify and isolate anomalous testbed behavior based on measurements from off- nominal operations. Results show that the Kalman filter-based digital twin can monitor individual powertrain components’ health for degradation or other changes in performance. The applicability of the presented digital twin approach to any hybrid- or fully-electrified powertrain is emphasized.

results.title: Ground Demonstration of Autonomous Robotic Laser Beam Welding for In-Space Servicing, Assembly, and Manufacturing
results.abstract: In-space servicing, assembly, and manufacturing (ISAM) missions require robotic systems that can perform precise joining and repair tasks despite communication latency, thermal variation, diverse lighting conditions, uncertain workpiece geometry, and limited crew intervention. This work presents the Lunar Assembly and Servicing by Autonomous Robotics (LASAR) system, a ground demonstration of autonomous robotic laser beam welding and additive manufacturing capabilities relevant to future ISAM missions. LASAR integrates PickNik MoveIt Pro with the Rocket Lab Robotics xLink robotic arm. Both technologies are also used by NASA’s Fly Foundational Robots mission, establishing a direct connection between terrestrial ISAM testing and future orbital robotic operations. The autonomy architecture combines model-based motion planning, collision-aware trajectory execution, autonomous seam detection, visual servoing for weld-tool alignment, coordinated laser and robot control, and supervisory remote operations. Operators at NASA Johnson Space Center (JSC) remotely commanded experiments performed at NASA Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC). Thermal-vacuum tests evaluated robotic welding at extreme temperatures from approximately −40 ◦C to 55 ◦C, while additional tests incorporated a wire-feed mechanism for additive deposition and weld repair. The demonstrations advance perception-guided manipulation, remote operations, and in-space welding capabilities needed for scalable ISAM infrastructure.

sourceIdentifiers.descriptor: CALIPSO Lidar Level 3 Cloud Occurrence Product Version 2.00

results.abstract: The CALIPSO lidar level 3 (L3) three-dimensional (3D) cloud occurrence product (COP) reports global distributions of cloud occurrence aggregated monthly on a uniform 3D spatial grid with 60 meter vertical resolution. The Version 2.00 release of L3 COP is derived from Version 5.00 Level 2 layer and profile products. L3 quality assurance (QA) filters are used to identify and reject low confidence or otherwise suspicious layers reported in the L2 data.  Rather than reporting monthly mean cloud occurrence, the product contains monthly counts of cloudy samples and cloud-free samples, with each sample representing one 60-meter range bin of a single shot profile. The product also contains counts for each of three cloud phases (ice, water, and unknown) for opaque clouds and for transparent clouds. For diagnostic purposes, counts of the samples rejected by the QA filters are also supplied.   Additional ice cloud information is provided by histograms of cloud layer optical depth (OD) for each grid cell. Background meteorological data (e.g., temperature, pressure, and relative humidity) and surface information such land/water surface types and snow sea ice extent coverage are also included.

results.title: An Unrivaled Asset: The NASA ER-2 as a Driver of Unique Scientific Innovation
results.abstract: The NASA ER-2 is a purpose-built version of the USAF U 2R high-altitude aircraft.  The ER 2 is capable of delivering over one ton of instrument payload to altitudes approaching 70,000 ft, well into the stratosphere, at subsonic speeds for an eight-hour flight. These aircraft uniquely enable a number of mission profiles important to NASA including targeted remote sensing and in-situ science, satellite calibration and validation, and instrument technology maturation.  The missions flown by these aircraft have been at the core of numerous ground-breaking discoveries, including the conclusive demonstration of the connection between chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) and the Antarctic ozone hole, as well as the discovery of novel electrical phenomena tied to thunderstorms.  In both these examples, the discoveries that resulted from the ER 2 flights were only possible because of the unrivaled flight altitude of the ER-2.  This manuscript, written based on collected responses from a community survey of the scientists, engineers, and crew who have been involved with these aircraft, examines the unique history, strengths, and weaknesses of the NASA ER-2 as a driver of unique scientific innovation.

results.title: Atmospheric Constituent Data Assimilation in NASA's Goddard Earth Observing System
results.abstract: Many of today's most significant and urgent scientific questions, including those about the impact of human activity on air quality and radiative forcing, require the synthesis of observations of atmospheric constituents and scientific theory. The past three decades have each seen a step-change in the coverage, accuracy, and precision of constituent observations, and hence the questions they can address, especially from the growing constellation of Earth-observing satellites. This paper is the first comprehensive description of the design and implementation of NASA’s Constituent Data Assimilation System (CoDAS), a software package for assimilating constituent observations into the Goddard Earth Observing System (GEOS), an integrated collection of Earth system models. CoDAS is a generalized, tracer-agnostic system that extends previous capabilities to assimilate multiple species from multiple sensors configurable at run time. Data assimilation provides a means of monitoring constituent changes, intercomparing heterogeneous types of observations, and reconciling data and models. Assimilation produces an optimal synthesis of the ingested data and model, taking advantage of the fact that the statistics of model-data differences are simpler than those of the observations themselves. The use of a model enables the propagation of information from all previous observations across space and time, which can improve estimates even where and when data are unavailable.
